extracted.intended_audience: users of the Metamath set.mm database; students and practitioners formalizing mathematics in Metamath / readers of a foundations-of-mathematics textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conventions for formalizing set theory and proofs in the Metamath set.mm database, including which axioms/definitions to introduce and how to write eliminable, conservative definitions and hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: First, and of utmost importance, the definition should not be creative, that is it should not allow an expression that previously qualified as a wff but was not provable, to become provable. Second, the definition should be eliminable, that is, there should exist an algorithmic method for converting any expression using the definition into a logically equivalent expression that previously qualified as a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In almost all cases definitions connect two expressions with either ↔ or =. Eliminating such a definition is a simple matter of substituting the expression on the left-hand side (definiendum) with the equivalent, more primitive expression on the right-hand side (definiens). The book emphasizes eliminability and non-strengthening of the language as essential requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminability / algorithmic expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: An important requirement for a definition is that there exist a straightforward (algorithmic) method for eliminating the abbreviation by expanding it into the more primitive symbol string that it represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elimination is what a human would do (or Metamath theorems implement). Examples: df-bi (biconditional) can be eliminated by theorem bii; most definitions are eliminable by substitution of the definiendum with the definiens.

rubrics_metrics.name: No strengthening of the language (conservativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should not strengthen the language: the extended language must be an eliminable and conservative extension of set theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservativity: every proof of a formula of the basic language in the extended system can be transformed into a proof in the basic system. Eliminability + conservativity means the extension is merely definitional and sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dummy variables must be effectively bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Often a definition has variables on the right-hand side which do not appear on the left-hand side; these are called dummy variables. Dummy variables may be used only if they are effectively bound, meaning the definition remains logically equivalent upon any substitution of the dummy variable with any other qualifying expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defining ⊥ as (ϕ ∧ ¬ϕ) — here ϕ is effectively bound because the definition remains equivalent when ϕ is replaced by any wff. When eliminating definitions with dummy variables, allow any allowable substitution (such as a new distinct variable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with definitions that extend existing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions that extend the meaning of existing symbols (e.g., extending = or ∈ to classes) are potentially dangerous and must be introduced carefully so they do not lead to contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: df-cleq extends equality to classes and presupposes the Axiom of Extensionality; thus df-cleq is introduced together with a hypothesis (df-cleq.1) so the use of Extensionality is explicit and traceable. The alternative would be to introduce a new symbol to avoid extending an existing one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize dependence on axioms / derive redundants
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize the number of axioms the development depends on; derive redundant axioms from others rather than treating them as primitive when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Axiom of the Null Set, Axiom of Pairing, and Axiom of Separation can be derived from other axioms and are treated as theorems in set.mm. The Metamath philosophy here is to keep the axiom set small and derive redundants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice usage policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Axiom of Choice is philosophically controversial; prefer proofs that do not use the Axiom of Choice where there is a known alternative, and use weaker axioms than the full Axiom of Choice when possible. That said, use the Axiom of Choice when needed because it is a powerful and widely accepted tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ZF set theory that includes the Axiom of Choice is called ZFC. The text notes AC is often used when needed but sometimes avoided in favor of weaker axioms; in some contexts (e.g., constructive logic) AC is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ↔ (biconditional) as definition connective
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of a separate 'Df.' marker, use the biconditional connective ↔ to state definitions so logic can manipulate definitions directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: df-bi uses ↔ to define the biconditional connective itself; theorem bii provides the elimination of ↔. This choice allows using logical theorems to handle definitions rather than a distinct definitional meta-symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions for hypotheses and variable restrictions ($d, $e, $a, $p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath uses compact $d, $e, $a, $p statements to express distinctness, non-occurrence, effective non-freeness, and assertion types; these have specific readings that must be followed when authoring or reading proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text: $d x y means assume x and y are distinct variables; $d x ϕ means assume x does not occur in ϕ; $e (ϕ → ∀x ϕ) should be read 'assume variable x is effectively not free in wff ϕ'; $e A ∈ V should be read 'assume class A is a set (i.e. exists)'. Also antecedents like $a (¬∀x x = y → ...) are used to mean 'if x and y are distinct variables, then...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit substitution device / restriction & hypothesis group
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the restriction and hypothesis group ($d x A, $d x ψ, $e (x = A → (ϕ ↔ ψ))) as a compact way to express that ψ results from the proper substitution of A for x in ϕ, avoiding explicit substitution in many proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implicit substitution convention shortens proofs. Sometimes $e (ψ → ∀x ψ) is used instead of $d x ψ when only effective non-freeness is needed. Use these devices with care as partly a matter of style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath syntactic conventions and notation placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting and notational conventions used in set.mm should be followed: the turnstile symbol is the first token of all assertions/hypotheses (non-syntax constructions); ascii Metamath source is placed below formulas; $f and $d statements may be omitted in the book's listing but are present in the database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conventions make Metamath statements machine-parseable and human-readable. The book shows ascii Metamath source under formulas and reminds the reader to consult show statements in the program for full $f and $d info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make hypotheses explicit when introducing extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition or construction relies on a non-logical axiom (e.g., Extensionality), include that axiom as a hypothesis so its use is visible in proof traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: df-cleq.1 states (∀x (x ∈ y ↔ x ∈ z) → y = z) as an explicit premise so that when df-cleq is used, the fact that Extensionality is assumed is visible via show trace_back.
